claim: The mode proliferation rate of a lab strain (BY4741) is 0.407 ± 0.011 h−1 during >2 years of data collection (n = 44 batches).
source: The data obtained are highly reproducible with mode proliferation rate of a lab strain being 0.407 ± 0.011 h−1, (mean ±sd) during >2 years of data collection (n = 44 batches; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements collected over 2 years with 44 batches, as stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Laboratory strains of budding yeast show substantial cell-to-cell variation in proliferation, with ~10% of cells forming a slow growing sub-population in defined growth medium.
source: Laboratory strains of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae showed substantial cell-to-cell variation in proliferation, with ~10% of cells forming a slow growing sub-population in defined growth medium (Figure 1A) (Levy et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and is also supported by citations to previous work by Levy et al., 2012 and Ziv et al., 2013.

claim: The slow growing sub-fraction is not unique to laboratory strains but exists in all natural and clinical isolates tested.
source: This slow growing sub-fraction is not unique to laboratory strains but exists in all natural and clinical isolates that we tested (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1) (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1, and is also supported by citation to Ziv et al., 2013.

claim: Growth of the culture for an additional 20 generations did not alter the proliferation rate distribution; the mixture of slow and fast proliferating cells is maintained.
source: Growth of the culture for an additional 20 generations did not alter the proliferation rate distribution; the mixture of slow and fast proliferating cells is maintained (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Proliferation is a stable heterogeneous phenotype within a population, with the amount of heterogeneity depending on the genetic background.
source: Proliferation is therefore a stable heterogeneous phenotype within a population, with the amount of heterogeneity depending on the genetic background.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations that proliferation heterogeneity is maintained over generations and varies across different genetic backgrounds (natural and clinical isolates).

claim: Reproducible data was obtained for 1520 gene deletions, with 1112 of these reducing the population proliferation rate.
source: We obtained reproducible data (where at least two replicate measurements showed good agreement) for 1520 deletions, with 1112 of these reducing the population proliferation rate in our experiment (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the genome-scale screen with statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1).

claim: Deletion strains with similar population proliferation rates often showed strikingly different degrees of intra-population heterogeneity.
source: Deletion strains with similar population proliferation rates often showed strikingly different degrees of intra-population heterogeneity (Fig, 2A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: ~39% of all mutants with a significant reduction in population proliferation rate showed significantly higher variation in mutation outcome compared to the WT strain.
source: At the single cell level,~39% of all mutants with a significant reduction in population proliferation rate (1112 mutants) showed significantly higher variation in mutation outcome compared to the WT strain (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1, after correcting for change in mode growth rate).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1).

claim: ~13% of mutants with significant reduction in population proliferation rate had the same mode growth rate as the WT strain while showing higher variability.
source: Among these mutants,~13% had the same mode growth rate as the WT strain while showing higher variability (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, FDR < 0.1).

claim: Almost all mutants (1111 of 1112 mutants) had a subset of cells proliferating at the same rate as the bulk of the wild-type (WT) population.
source: However, almost all mutants (1111 of 1112 mutants) had a subset of cells proliferating at the same rate as the bulk of the wild-type (WT) population (one sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test for overlap with bulk WT distribution differing from zero, FDR < 0.1; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing (one sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test, FDR < 0.1) and shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A highly variable outcome is the normal outcome for proliferation rate at the single cell level when a non-essential gene is inactivated.
source: Thus, a highly variable outcome is actually the normal outcome for proliferation rate at the single cell level when a non-essential gene is inactivated (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that almost all mutants show incomplete penetrance, as shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Deletions causing the largest increase in the fraction of slow proliferating cells were highly enriched for nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins.
source: Deletions causing the largest increase in the fraction of slow proliferating cells were highly enriched for nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of experimental data, as shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: Among mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate, ~30% localized to mitochondria (~1.2 fold enrichment).
source: Among the mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate (Figure 2E, magenta), ~30% localized to mitochondria (~1.2 fold enrichment),~13% localized to the mitochondrial envelope (>1.6 fold enrichment) and ~4.6% were involved in cellular respiration (~2-fold enrichment).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of experimental data, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ~13% of mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate localized to the mitochondrial envelope (>1.6 fold enrichment).
source: Among the mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate (Figure 2E, magenta), ~30% localized to mitochondria (~1.2 fold enrichment),~13% localized to the mitochondrial envelope (>1.6 fold enrichment) and ~4.6% were involved in cellular respiration (~2-fold enrichment).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of experimental data, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ~4.6% of mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate were involved in cellular respiration (~2-fold enrichment).
source: Among the mutants that increased the slow fraction but also reduced mode growth rate (Figure 2E, magenta), ~30% localized to mitochondria (~1.2 fold enrichment),~13% localized to the mitochondrial envelope (>1.6 fold enrichment) and ~4.6% were involved in cellular respiration (~2-fold enrichment).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of experimental data, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of genes that localized to the mitochondrial envelope resulted in a large increase in slow fraction and noise.
source: In particular, deletion of genes that localized to the mitochondrial envelope resulted in a large increase in slow fraction and noise (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Mutations that affect mitochondria, and in particular the mitochondria membrane, increase heterogeneity.
source: Mutations that affect mitochondria, and in particular the mitochondria membrane, increase heterogeneity, suggesting that heterogeneity in proliferation might be associated with cell-to-cell variation in mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that deletion of mitochondrial genes, especially those localized to the mitochondrial envelope, increase proliferation heterogeneity.

claim: Total mitochondria amount varied little across WT cells and five deletion strains with very different proliferation distributions.
source: Total mitochondria amount varied little across the strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), ruling out cell-to-cell variation in segregation of the organelle as a driver of heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry measurements of Mitotracker green intensity shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Cell-to-cell variation in segregation of mitochondria is ruled out as a driver of heterogeneity.
source: Total mitochondria amount varied little across the strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), ruling out cell-to-cell variation in segregation of the organelle as a driver of heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that mitochondrial amount does not vary substantially across strains with different proliferation heterogeneity.

claim: Signal from the mitochondria membrane potential dye TMRE varied substantially across WT, mutants and natural strains.
source: However, signal from the mitochondria membrane potential dye TMRE varied substantially across WT, mutants and natural strains (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry measurements of TMRE intensity shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The mitochondria membrane potential – but not their amount – might be driving proliferation heterogeneity.
source: This suggested that the mitochondria membrane potential – but not their amount – might be driving proliferation heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations that mitochondrial amount does not vary but TMRE signal (membrane potential) does vary across strains with different proliferation heterogeneity.

claim: The population with high TMRE was highly enriched for slowly proliferating cells.
source: The population with high TMRE was highly enriched for slowly proliferating cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sorting cells by TMRE intensity and measuring proliferation rates, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The high TMRE fraction was strongly enriched for respiration deficient cells.
source: This same fraction was also strongly enriched for respiration deficient cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from plating sorted cells on glycerol plates and counting respiration deficient colonies, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Strong enrichment for slow proliferation and respiration deficiency was observed for cells with high TMRE in gene deletion strains and in natural isolates.
source: This strong enrichment for slow proliferation and respiration deficiency was also observed for the cells with high TMRE in gene deletion strains and in natural isolates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The percentage of slowly proliferating cells showed a high correlation with the percentage of respiration-deficient cells across all datasets.
source: Across all datasets, the percentage of slowly proliferating cells showed a high correlation with the percentage of respiration-deficient cells (Figure 3E,F) as well as with the percentage of high TMRE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation across multiple strains, as shown in Figure 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The percentage of slowly proliferating cells showed a high correlation with the percentage of high TMRE cells across all datasets.
source: Across all datasets, the percentage of slowly proliferating cells showed a high correlation with the percentage of respiration-deficient cells (Figure 3E,F) as well as with the percentage of high TMRE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation across multiple strains, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mtDNA copy number was substantially lower in the cells with high TMRE.
source: Although cell-to-cell variation in mitochondrial amount did not predict proliferation rate variation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), mtDNA copy number was substantially lower in the cells with high TMRE (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting a likely role of mtDNA copy number in defining mitochondrial membrane potential and ultimately, in generation of growth rate heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in sorted cells, as shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: mtDNA copy number likely plays a role in defining mitochondrial membrane potential and in generation of growth rate heterogeneity.
source: Although cell-to-cell variation in mitochondrial amount did not predict proliferation rate variation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), mtDNA copy number was substantially lower in the cells with high TMRE (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting a likely role of mtDNA copy number in defining mitochondrial membrane potential and ultimately, in generation of growth rate heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that cells with high TMRE (high membrane potential) have lower mtDNA copy number.

claim: Overexpression of Mip1 gene increased mtDNA copy number 3-fold.
source: To establish a causal relationship between mtDNA copy number and slow growth, we introduced an extra copy of the mitochondrial DNA polymerase Mip1 (Genga et al., 1986), which increased mtDNA copy number 3-fold (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in cells overexpressing Mip1, as shown in Figure 4B, and is also supported by citation to Genga et al., 1986.

claim: Overexpression of Mip1 reduced both the fraction of slow proliferating and respiration-deficient cells and the fraction of cells with high TMRE signal.
source: This reduced both the fraction of slow proliferating and respiration-deficient cells and the fraction of cells with high TMRE signal (Figure 4C,D), suggesting that variation in mtDNA copy number can be causal for variation in both mitochondrial membrane potential and proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy and flow cytometry measurements in cells overexpressing Mip1, as shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Variation in mtDNA copy number can be causal for variation in both mitochondrial membrane potential and proliferation.
source: This reduced both the fraction of slow proliferating and respiration-deficient cells and the fraction of cells with high TMRE signal (Figure 4C,D), suggesting that variation in mtDNA copy number can be causal for variation in both mitochondrial membrane potential and proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that increasing mtDNA copy number by overexpressing Mip1 reduces slow proliferation, respiration deficiency, and high TMRE signal.

claim: Knocking out Mip1 gene led to complete loss of mtDNA and resulted in completely slow growing yeast population compared to WT.
source: Consistent with an effect of mtDNA copy number on growth, knocking out of Mip1 gene led to complete loss of mtDNA and resulted in completely slow growing yeast population compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D) (Genga et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D and is also supported by citation to Genga et al., 1986.

claim: mtDNA copy number showed a strong negative correlation with the percentage of slow proliferating cells across mutants.
source: Furthermore, mtDNA copy number showed a strong negative correlation with the percentage of slow proliferating cells across mutants (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation across multiple mutant strains, as shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Forcing cells to respire by pre-growing them on ethanol as the sole carbon source prior to growth in glucose decreased the fraction of slowly proliferating cells.
source: Finally, forcing cells to respire by pre-growing them on ethanol as the sole carbon source prior to growth in glucose decreased the fraction of slowly proliferating cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy measurements of cells pre-grown on ethanol, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential, which can be caused by mtDNA copy number reduction below a threshold and other mechanisms, is the underlying cause of slow growth in individual cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that alterations in mitochondrial membrane potential, which can be caused by mtDNA copy number reduction below a threshold and other mechanisms is the underlying cause of slow growth in individual cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations including the correlation between TMRE signal and slow growth, the effect of mtDNA copy number on TMRE signal and slow growth, and the effect of pre-growth on ethanol on slow growth.

claim: Cells with high TMRE have low expression of respiratory and proliferation-associated genes.
source: Cells with high TMRE have low expression of respiratory and proliferation-associated genes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cells with high TMRE exhibit a DNA damage response.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of slow proliferating cells (Yaakov et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2015), they also exhibit a DNA damage response (Figure 5B) and signs of iron starvation (Figure 5C), which has previously been reported for respiration deficient cells (Veatch et al., 2009; Puig et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells showing expression of DNA damage response genes, as shown in Figure 5B, and is also supported by citations to previous work by Yaakov et al., 2017 and van Dijk et al., 2015.

claim: Cells with high TMRE exhibit signs of iron starvation.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of slow proliferating cells (Yaakov et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2015), they also exhibit a DNA damage response (Figure 5B) and signs of iron starvation (Figure 5C), which has previously been reported for respiration deficient cells (Veatch et al., 2009; Puig et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells showing expression of iron deficiency genes, as shown in Figure 5C, and is also supported by citations to previous work by Veatch et al., 2009 and Puig et al., 2005.

claim: Cells with intermediate TMRE have very similar proliferation distributions to cells with low potential.
source: Cells with intermediate TMRE have very similar proliferation distributions to cells with low potential (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy measurements of sorted cells, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells with intermediate TMRE have substantially different gene expression compared to cells with low potential.
source: However, their gene expression was substantially different (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), including reduced expression of respiratory genes in cells with intermediate TMRE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Cells with high TMRE were more sensitive to heat shock.
source: However, cells with high TMRE were more sensitive to heat shock as well as to oxidative stress (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and expressed some stress-response genes at lower levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from heat shock survival assays on sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cells with high TMRE were more sensitive to oxidative stress.
source: However, cells with high TMRE were more sensitive to heat shock as well as to oxidative stress (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and expressed some stress-response genes at lower levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from hydrogen peroxide survival assays on sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cells with high TMRE expressed some stress-response genes at lower levels.
source: However, cells with high TMRE were more sensitive to heat shock as well as to oxidative stress (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and expressed some stress-response genes at lower levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In several species of fungi, complete loss of mitochondria is associated with elevated tolerance to some antifungal drugs.
source: Moreover, in several species of fungi, complete loss of mitochondria is associated with elevated tolerance to some antifungal drugs (Hallstrom and Moye-Rowley, 2000; Brun et al., 2004; Zhang and Moye-Rowley, 2001) and respiration deficient strains are often isolated from drug-treated patients (Bouchara et al., 2000; Ferrari et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hallstrom and Moye-Rowley, 2000; Brun et al., 2004; and Zhang and Moye-Rowley, 2001.

claim: Respiration deficient strains are often isolated from drug-treated patients.
source: Moreover, in several species of fungi, complete loss of mitochondria is associated with elevated tolerance to some antifungal drugs (Hallstrom and Moye-Rowley, 2000; Brun et al., 2004; Zhang and Moye-Rowley, 2001) and respiration deficient strains are often isolated from drug-treated patients (Bouchara et al., 2000; Ferrari et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Bouchara et al., 2000; Ferrari et al., 2011; and Peng et al., 2012.

claim: Cells with high TMRE were ~5–7 fold more resistant to high concentrations of fluconazole.
source: We found that cells with high TMRE were ~5–7 fold more resistant to high concentrations of fluconazole (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluconazole survival assays on sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The cells surviving fluconazole treatment included a sub-fraction able to respire.
source: The cells surviving fluconazole treatment included a sub-fraction able to respire (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from plating fluconazole-surviving cells on glycerol plates, as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cell-to-cell variation in mitochondrial membrane potential is an important predictor of cell-to-cell variation in drug resistance.
source: Cell-to-cell variation in mitochondrial membrane potential is therefore also an important predictor of cell-to-cell variation in drug resistance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that cells with high TMRE show increased resistance to fluconazole.

claim: Fluconazole targets the cytochrome P450 14α-sterol demethylase enzyme (ERG11), resulting in depletion of ergosterol, a key component of the yeast cell membrane.
source: Fluconazole targets the cytochrome P450 14α-sterol demethylase enzyme (ERG11), resulting in depletion of ergosterol, a key component of the yeast cell membrane (Hitchcock et al., 1990; Ghannoum and Rice, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hitchcock et al., 1990 and Ghannoum and Rice, 1999, representing established knowledge about fluconazole mechanism of action.

claim: Survival in fluconazole has been previously reported to depend on the multidrug transporter PDR5.
source: Survival in fluconazole has been previously reported to depend on the multidrug transporter PDR5 (Brun et al., 2004; Parsons et al., 2004; Miranda et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Brun et al., 2004; Parsons et al., 2004; and Miranda et al., 2010.

claim: High TMRE cells had significantly higher level of PDR5 expression.
source: High TMRE cells had significantly higher level of PDR5 expression (Figure 5G; Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) as well as higher expression of the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: High TMRE cells had higher expression of the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway.
source: High TMRE cells had significantly higher level of PDR5 expression (Figure 5G; Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) as well as higher expression of the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The elevated expression of PDR5 in the high membrane potential cells was dependent on the PDR3 transcription factor.
source: Consistent with previous work (Katzmann et al., 1994; Delaveau et al., 1994), the elevated expression of PDR5 in the high membrane potential cells was dependent on the PDR3 transcription factor (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry measurements of PDR5-GFP in pdr3Δ cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, and is also supported by citations to previous work by Katzmann et al., 1994 and Delaveau et al., 1994.

claim: The increased resistance in fluconazole of high TMRE cells is likely to be mediated, at least in part, by increased expression of a multidrug transporter.
source: Thus, the increased resistance in fluconazole of high TMRE cells is likely to be mediated, at least in part, by increased expression of a multidrug transporter.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations that high TMRE cells have increased PDR5 expression and increased fluconazole resistance, combined with previous knowledge that PDR5 mediates fluconazole resistance.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential – but not the amount of mitochondria – varies substantially across individual yeast cells.
source: In summary, we have shown here that mitochondrial membrane potential – but not the amount of mitochondria – varies substantially across individual yeast cells and that this is associated with cell-to-cell heterogeneity in proliferation, mutation outcome, and stress and drug resistance.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the study showing variation in TMRE signal but not Mitotracker green signal across cells.

claim: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential is associated with cell-to-cell heterogeneity in proliferation, mutation outcome, and stress and drug resistance.
source: In summary, we have shown here that mitochondrial membrane potential – but not the amount of mitochondria – varies substantially across individual yeast cells and that this is associated with cell-to-cell heterogeneity in proliferation, mutation outcome, and stress and drug resistance.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the study showing correlations between TMRE signal and various phenotypes.

claim: Laboratory strains of yeast have long been known to generate respiratory deficient 'petite' colonies at quite high frequency.
source: Laboratory strains of yeast have long been known to generate respiratory deficient 'petite' colonies at quite high frequency (Dimitrov et al., 2009; Nagley and Linnane, 1970; Evans et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Dimitrov et al., 2009; Nagley and Linnane, 1970; and Evans et al., 1985, representing established knowledge.

claim: A slow growing sub-population of cells was observed in all the laboratory, natural, and clinical strains tested.
source: However, a slow growing sub-population of cells was observed in all the laboratory, natural, and clinical strains that we tested (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy measurements across multiple strains, as shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Other causes of slow growth beyond mitochondrial genes will exist.
source: Although, mitochondrial genes showed the strongest enrichment for an increased slow fraction in our gene deletion screen, other causes of slow growth will, of course, also exist.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that not all genes affecting slow growth are mitochondrial genes.

claim: Deletions of genes associated with chromosome segregation and nucleus organization also affected heterogeneity but had no apparent relation to mitochondrial function.
source: For example, deletions of genes associated with chromosome segregation and nucleus organization also affected heterogeneity but had no apparent relation to mitochondrial function.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of experimental data from the gene deletion screen.

claim: Environmental conditions, both during growth prior to microscopy, and during microscopy, are likely to affect heterogeneity.
source: Environmental conditions, both during growth prior to microscopy, and during microscopy, are likely to affect heterogeneity; pre-growth in ethanol reduces proliferation heterogeneity (Figure 4F), presumably due to selection for cells with well-functioning mitochondria and high mtDNA copy number.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that pre-growth on ethanol reduces slow fraction, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pre-growth in ethanol reduces proliferation heterogeneity, presumably due to selection for cells with well-functioning mitochondria and high mtDNA copy number.
source: Environmental conditions, both during growth prior to microscopy, and during microscopy, are likely to affect heterogeneity; pre-growth in ethanol reduces proliferation heterogeneity (Figure 4F), presumably due to selection for cells with well-functioning mitochondria and high mtDNA copy number.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, with the mechanism being speculative.

claim: Previous theoretical studies have proposed that variability in the partitioning of cellular components could lead to heterogeneity.
source: Previous theoretical studies have proposed that variability in the partitioning of cellular components could lead to heterogeneity (Birky and Skavaril, 1984; Huh and Paulsson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work by Birky and Skavaril, 1984 and Huh and Paulsson, 2011.

claim: Prior experimental work on the fidelity of mitochondria inheritance has shown it to be high, suggesting it is likely to be of little phenotypic consequence for single cells.
source: However, prior experimental work on the fidelity of mitochondria inheritance has shown it to be high, suggesting it is likely to be of little phenotypic consequence for single cells (Jajoo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Jajoo et al., 2016.

claim: Cell-to-cell variation in the state of the organelle can be high and predicts phenotypic variation among single cells.
source: In contrast, we have shown here that cell-to-cell variation in the state of the organelle can be high and predicts phenotypic variation among single cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the study showing variation in mitochondrial membrane potential and its correlation with phenotypic variation.

claim: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential has been shown to exist in isogenic yeast populations.
source: Although variation in mitochondrial membrane potential has been shown to exist in isogenic yeast populations (Fehrmann et al., 2013), here we have linked such variations to heterogeneity in growth and drug resistance phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Fehrmann et al., 2013.

claim: This study has linked variation in mitochondrial membrane potential to heterogeneity in growth and drug resistance phenotypes.
source: Although variation in mitochondrial membrane potential has been shown to exist in isogenic yeast populations (Fehrmann et al., 2013), here we have linked such variations to heterogeneity in growth and drug resistance phenotypes.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the study showing correlations between TMRE signal and growth and drug resistance phenotypes.

claim: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential was related to variation in mtDNA copy number in individual cells.
source: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential was related to variation in mtDNA copy number in individual cells, but we do not currently know if this is the only – or even the most common – cause of variation in the state of the organelle across single cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between TMRE signal and mtDNA copy number, and the causal effect of manipulating mtDNA copy number on TMRE signal.

claim: It is not currently known if mtDNA copy number variation is the only – or even the most common – cause of variation in the state of the organelle across single cells.
source: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential was related to variation in mtDNA copy number in individual cells, but we do not currently know if this is the only – or even the most common – cause of variation in the state of the organelle across single cells.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the limitation of current knowledge based on the experimental findings.

claim: The list of gene deletions that alter growth heterogeneity provide a rich resource for future work to track down the upstream, proximal causes of cell-to-cell variation in organelle functional state.
source: Future work will be required to track down the upstream, proximal causes of this cell-to-cell variation in organelle functional state. The list of gene deletions that alter growth heterogeneity that we have reported here provide a rich resource for this future work.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data generated in the study (the genome-scale screen) and speculation about its future utility.

claim: Three different methods have been used to identify slow-proliferating yeast within a population: GFP tagged TSL1, GFP tagged HSP12, and FitFlow.
source: In addition to the TMRE method we used, three different methods have now been used to identify slow-proliferating yeast within a population: GFP tagged TSL1, GFP tagged HSP12, and FitFlow, a direct method (Levy et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; van Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Levy et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; and van Dijk et al., 2015.

claim: Early work on proliferation heterogeneity in yeast has correlated expression noise in a stress response gene with proliferation heterogeneity.
source: For example, early work on proliferation heterogeneity in yeast has correlated expression noise in a stress response gene with proliferation heterogeneity (Levy et al., 2012) with this ultimately linked to the variation in the activity of the Ras/cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) pathway and its target transcription factors MSN2 and MSN4 in individual yeast cells leading to variation in expression of downstream stress response genes (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Levy et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2018.

claim: Variation in the activity of the Ras/cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) pathway and its target transcription factors MSN2 and MSN4 in individual yeast cells leads to variation in expression of downstream stress response genes.
source: For example, early work on proliferation heterogeneity in yeast has correlated expression noise in a stress response gene with proliferation heterogeneity (Levy et al., 2012) with this ultimately linked to the variation in the activity of the Ras/cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) pathway and its target transcription factors MSN2 and MSN4 in individual yeast cells leading to variation in expression of downstream stress response genes (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Li et al., 2018.

claim: pde2 and ira2 cells have a reduced fraction of slow growing microcolonies.
source: Some of our results are identical to that of Li et al. (Li et al., 2018); we also find that pde2 and ira2 cells have a reduced fraction of slow growing microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the gene deletion screen and is consistent with previous work by Li et al., 2018.

claim: TSL1 mRNA expression is lower in the high TMRE sub-population.
source: Importantly, TSL1 mRNA expression is lower in the high TMRE sub-population, as are the MSN2/MSN4 targets CTT1, DDR2 and HSP12.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells.

claim: The MSN2/MSN4 targets CTT1, DDR2 and HSP12 have lower expression in the high TMRE sub-population.
source: Importantly, TSL1 mRNA expression is lower in the high TMRE sub-population, as are the MSN2/MSN4 targets CTT1, DDR2 and HSP12.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from sorted cells.

claim: Other studies have suggested a role for the DNA damage response in the generation and or maintenance of proliferation heterogeneity.
source: Other studies have suggested a role for the DNA damage response in the generation and or maintenance of proliferation heterogeneity (Yaakov et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Yaakov et al., 2017 and van Dijk et al., 2015.

claim: The slow growing sub-populations in an isogenic yeast population are primarily driven by loss of mitochondrial function in lab, natural and clinically-isolated yeast strains.
source: Results from our screen show that the slow growing sub-populations in an isogenic yeast population are primarily driven by loss of mitochondrial function in lab, natural and clinically-isolated yeast strains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings that mitochondrial genes are enriched among deletions increasing slow fraction, and that high TMRE cells (which are slow growing) are enriched for respiration deficiency.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial function leads to a loss of respiration capability and induced DNA damage response.
source: Loss of mitochondrial function leads to a loss of respiration capability and induced DNA damage response, consistent with previous reports (Yaakov et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing showing DNA damage response in high TMRE cells, and is consistent with previous work by Yaakov et al., 2017 and van Dijk et al., 2015.

claim: There are multiple types of slow-proliferating cells.
source: Taken together, results across all four studies suggest that there are multiple types of slow-proliferating cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of results across multiple studies showing different characteristics of slow-proliferating cells.

claim: Prior work on the causes of variation in proliferation rates, stress and drug resistance, and mutation outcome across individuals and individual cells has focused on fluctuations in gene expression as causative influences.
source: Prior work on the causes of variation in proliferation rates, stress and drug resistance, and mutation outcome across individuals and individual cells has focused on fluctuations in gene expression as causative influences (Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017; Shaffer et al., 2017; Burga et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2010; Eldar et al., 2009; Li et al., 2018; Rotem et al., 2010; Battich et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: In yeast, variation in an organelle is strongly associated with heterogeneity in gene expression across single cells.
source: Here we have shown that, in yeast, variation in an organelle is strongly associated with heterogeneity in gene expression across single cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing showing different gene expression patterns in cells sorted by TMRE signal.

claim: In animals, inherited and somatic genetic variation in the mitochondrial genome can act as an important modifier of phenotypic variation.
source: In animals, inherited and somatic genetic variation in the mitochondrial genome can act as an important modifier of phenotypic variation (Haag-Liautard et al., 2008; Kujoth et al., 2007; Tyynismaa and Suomalainen, 2009; Kauppila et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: Recent work has revealed substantial variation in mtDNA copy number across human tumors.
source: Recent work has also revealed substantial variation in mtDNA copy number across human tumors (Reznik et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Reznik et al., 2016.

claim: In mammalian cells, mitochondrial variability has been suggested to be an important influence on cell-to-cell variation in gene expression and splicing.
source: Moreover, in mammalian cells, mitochondrial variability has been suggested to be an important influence on cell-to-cell variation in gene expression and splicing (Johnston et al., 2012; Guantes et al., 2015; Guantes et al., 2016) and to influence variability in cell death by modulating apoptotic gene expression (Márquez-Jurado et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Johnston et al., 2012; Guantes et al., 2015; and Guantes et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondrial variability influences variability in cell death by modulating apoptotic gene expression.
source: Moreover, in mammalian cells, mitochondrial variability has been suggested to be an important influence on cell-to-cell variation in gene expression and splicing (Johnston et al., 2012; Guantes et al., 2015; Guantes et al., 2016) and to influence variability in cell death by modulating apoptotic gene expression (Márquez-Jurado et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Márquez-Jurado et al., 2018.

claim: Cellular organelles, in general, and mitochondria, in particular, play important roles in the generation of heterogeneity among individual cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest important roles for cellular organelles, in general, and mitochondria, in particular, in the generation of heterogeneity among individual cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings in this study combined with previous work cited showing roles for mitochondria in various organisms.

claim: It will be important to test the extent to which cell-to-cell variation in the state of mitochondria and other organelles also contributes to variable phenotypic outcomes, mutation effects, and drug resistance in human cells, including in cancer.
source: In future work, therefore, it will be important to test the extent to which cell-to-cell variation in the state of mitochondria and other organelles also contributes to variable phenotypic outcomes, mutation effects, and drug resistance in human cells, including in cancer.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future research directions based on the findings in yeast.

claim: Isogenic populations often exhibit considerable phenotypic heterogeneity even in an identical environment.
source: Isogenic populations often exhibit considerable phenotypic heterogeneity even in an identical environment.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Variation in proliferation rate is a common phenotypic variation observed in isogenic populations of microbial and mammalian cells, including cancer cells.
source: One common phenotypic variation that has been observed in isogenic populations of microbial and mammalian cells, including cancer cells is variation in proliferation rate (Sandler et al., 2015; Fridman et al., 2014; Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017; Ferrezuelo et al., 2012; Polymenis and Schmidt, 1999; Gupta et al., 2011; Kiviet et al., 2014; Roesch et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: Phenotypic variations that are often coupled with variation in proliferation rate are the abilities of an individual cell to survive stress and drug treatment.
source: Phenotypic variations that are often coupled with variation in proliferation rate are the abilities of an individual cell to survive stress and drug treatment (Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Levy et al., 2012 and Yaakov et al., 2017.

claim: The existence of 'persister' cells in microbial populations is well known and poses a significant challenge for antibiotic treatment.
source: In this regard, the existence of 'persister' cells in microbial populations is well known and poses a significant challenge for antibiotic treatment (Fridman et al., 2014; Balaban et al., 2004; Kussell et al., 2005; Wakamoto et al., 2013; LaFleur et al., 2006; Bojsen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors, representing established knowledge.

claim: Individual cells in tumors have been shown to vary in their ability to survive anticancer drugs and can lead to drug-resistant populations.
source: Similarly, individual cells in tumors have been shown to vary in their ability to survive anticancer drugs and can lead to drug-resistant populations (Shaffer et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2010; Ramirez et al., 2016; Hata et al., 2016; Rego et al., 2017; Márquez-Jurado et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: Recent advances in single-cell techniques are revealing the extent of transcriptomic and metabolic differences among isogenic cells.
source: Recent advances in single-cell techniques are revealing the extent of transcriptomic and metabolic differences among isogenic cells (Dey et al., 2015; Trapnell, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Dey et al., 2015 and Trapnell, 2015.

claim: The existence of heterogeneity in gene expression in isogenic microbial and animal populations has been shown – to some extent – to underlie the variable outcome of mutations.
source: The existence of such heterogeneity in gene expression in isogenic microbial and animal populations has been shown – to some extent – to underlie the variable outcome of mutations (Dickinson et al., 2016; Burga et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2010; Eldar et al., 2009; Horvitz and Sulston, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: Incomplete mutation penetrance and variable expressivity is common in human disease.
source: Incomplete mutation penetrance and variable expressivity is also common in human disease (Cooper et al., 2013; Zlotogora, 2003; Giudicessi and Ackerman, 2013; Otterson et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors, representing established knowledge.

claim: Heterogeneity can arise due to stochastic fluctuations in biological processes taking place inside cells.
source: Heterogeneity can arise due to stochastic fluctuations in biological processes taking place inside cells.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Stochastic fluctuations can happen due to the small numbers of molecules involved in processes such as transcription.
source: This can happen due to the small numbers of molecules involved in processes such as transcription (Berg, 1978; Rigney, 1979; Cookson et al., 2010) or during stochastic partitioning of cellular components during cell division (Birky and Skavaril, 1984; Huh and Paulsson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Berg, 1978; Rigney, 1979; and Cookson et al., 2010.

claim: Stochastic fluctuations can happen during stochastic partitioning of cellular components during cell division.
source: This can happen due to the small numbers of molecules involved in processes such as transcription (Berg, 1978; Rigney, 1979; Cookson et al., 2010) or during stochastic partitioning of cellular components during cell division (Birky and Skavaril, 1984; Huh and Paulsson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Birky and Skavaril, 1984 and Huh and Paulsson, 2011.

claim: Genetic variation has been shown to influence proliferation heterogeneity.
source: Although genetic variation has been shown to influence proliferation heterogeneity (Ziv et al., 2013) and cell-to-cell variation in the expression level of single genes and levels of metabolite has been correlated with variation in proliferation rate and stress and drug resistance (Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017; Shaffer et al., 2017; Burga et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2010; Eldar et al., 2009; Li et al., 2018; Rotem et al., 2010; Battich et al., 2015), the true underlying causes of such phenotypic heterogeneity are poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Ziv et al., 2013.

claim: Cell-to-cell variation in the expression level of single genes and levels of metabolite has been correlated with variation in proliferation rate and stress and drug resistance.
source: Although genetic variation has been shown to influence proliferation heterogeneity (Ziv et al., 2013) and cell-to-cell variation in the expression level of single genes and levels of metabolite has been correlated with variation in proliferation rate and stress and drug resistance (Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017; Shaffer et al., 2017; Burga et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2010; Eldar et al., 2009; Li et al., 2018; Rotem et al., 2010; Battich et al., 2015), the true underlying causes of such phenotypic heterogeneity are poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: The true underlying causes of phenotypic heterogeneity are poorly understood.
source: Although genetic variation has been shown to influence proliferation heterogeneity (Ziv et al., 2013) and cell-to-cell variation in the expression level of single genes and levels of metabolite has been correlated with variation in proliferation rate and stress and drug resistance (Levy et al., 2012; Yaakov et al., 2017; Shaffer et al., 2017; Burga et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2010; Eldar et al., 2009; Li et al., 2018; Rotem et al., 2010; Battich et al., 2015), the true underlying causes of such phenotypic heterogeneity are poorly understood.
evidence: The claim represents the motivation for the study based on the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Variation in mitochondrial membrane potential is an important determinant of phenotypic heterogeneity in individual cells.
source: We present evidence that the variation in mitochondrial membrane potential is an important determinant of phenotypic heterogeneity in individual cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential impacts gene expression and stress tolerance and drug resistance in individual cells.
source: We also show that mitochondrial membrane potential impacts gene expression and stress tolerance and drug resistance in individual cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the study showing correlations between TMRE signal and gene expression, stress tolerance, and drug resistance.

claim: An organelle plays an important role in generating phenotypic heterogeneity across individual cells in a homogenous environment.
source: Taken together, our work suggests an important role for an organelle in generating phenotypic heterogeneity across individual cells in a homogenous environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing the role of mitochondrial membrane potential in phenotypic heterogeneity.

claim: Slow growing microbes and cancer cells often have increased drug resistance.
source: Slow growing microbes and cancer cells often have increased drug resistance (Fridman et al., 2014; Yaakov et al., 2017; Wakamoto et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2016; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: In bacteria and yeast, slow growing cells can have increased stress resistance.
source: In bacteria (Ihssen and Egli, 2004) and yeast (Levy et al., 2012; Brauer et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2009), slow growing cells can have increased stress resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by multiple authors.

claim: Across mutants, there is a strong inverse relationship between mean growth rate and noise (co-efficient of variation).
source: Across mutants, we observed a strong inverse relationship between mean growth rate and noise (co-efficient of variation) (Figure 2C), as has been observed for gene expression (Newman et al., 2006; Bar-Even et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with previous observations for gene expression cited.

claim: A strong inverse relationship between mean and noise has been observed for gene expression.
source: Across mutants, we observed a strong inverse relationship between mean growth rate and noise (co-efficient of variation) (Figure 2C), as has been observed for gene expression (Newman et al., 2006; Bar-Even et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Newman et al., 2006 and Bar-Even et al., 2006.
